title: Interview frame
summary: Spend the hour in a fixed order and leave time to name the bottleneck.

parts.rule: Give the interview a visible sequence: clarify scope and quality targets, estimate scale, define the external API and core data, walk one write and one read, then deepen the first important bottleneck or failure. Announce assumptions and check them with the interviewer. Reserve the final minutes to summarize tradeoffs and name what you would address next.
parts.why: Without pacing, an answer can spend half the session on one schema detail or accumulate components that have no requirement behind them. A shared outline lets the interviewer redirect you and makes each decision traceable. The frame is not a script to recite; it is a way to protect time for the hard reasoning.
parts.example: For a 45-minute URL-shortener discussion, spend minutes 0–5 confirming create, redirect, and disable, plus a p95 redirect target below 100 ms. Park analytics unless it changes the requested design. In minutes 5–10, assume 10 creates and 1,000 redirects per second on average, a 3× peak, and roughly 315 million new rows per year. In minutes 10–15, define POST /v1/links, GET /{code}, and DELETE /v1/links/{code}; sketch Link(code, destination_url, owner_id, created_at, disabled_at). In minutes 15–27, walk create to a committed primary row and redirect through cache-aside to a primary-key lookup. In minutes 27–38, choose one deep dive: 7-character code collisions, cache invalidation after disable, or replica staleness. Use the remaining time to cover cache and database failure, restate why sharding is not yet required, and summarize the consistency tradeoff. If the interviewer asks about abuse at minute 20, adjust the plan openly rather than ignoring the question or abandoning the whole structure. Every box on the final diagram should now have a job tied to a requirement or estimate.
parts.use: Use the frame for open-ended system questions and adapt the time boxes to the interview length. Keep a small list of assumptions and parked features. When discussion goes deep early, note where you are in the outline and agree on which later section will be shortened.
parts.refuse: Do not select vendors, queues, or shards before the workload and access paths exist. Avoid designing every optional feature or a multi-region disaster plan for a single-region MVP unless asked. A polished diagram is incomplete if no request was traced, no failure was considered, or no bottleneck was chosen for deeper analysis.

body:
Rule. Give the interview a visible sequence: clarify scope and quality targets, estimate scale, define the external API and core data, walk one write and one read, then deepen the first important bottleneck or failure. Announce assumptions and check them with the interviewer. Reserve the final minutes to summarize tradeoffs and name what you would address next.

Why it matters. Without pacing, an answer can spend half the session on one schema detail or accumulate components that have no requirement behind them. A shared outline lets the interviewer redirect you and makes each decision traceable. The frame is not a script to recite; it is a way to protect time for the hard reasoning.

Worked example. For a 45-minute URL-shortener discussion, spend minutes 0–5 confirming create, redirect, and disable, plus a p95 redirect target below 100 ms. Park analytics unless it changes the requested design. In minutes 5–10, assume 10 creates and 1,000 redirects per second on average, a 3× peak, and roughly 315 million new rows per year. In minutes 10–15, define POST /v1/links, GET /{code}, and DELETE /v1/links/{code}; sketch Link(code, destination_url, owner_id, created_at, disabled_at). In minutes 15–27, walk create to a committed primary row and redirect through cache-aside to a primary-key lookup. In minutes 27–38, choose one deep dive: 7-character code collisions, cache invalidation after disable, or replica staleness. Use the remaining time to cover cache and database failure, restate why sharding is not yet required, and summarize the consistency tradeoff. If the interviewer asks about abuse at minute 20, adjust the plan openly rather than ignoring the question or abandoning the whole structure. Every box on the final diagram should now have a job tied to a requirement or estimate.

[[diagram:flow]]

When to use. Use the frame for open-ended system questions and adapt the time boxes to the interview length. Keep a small list of assumptions and parked features. When discussion goes deep early, note where you are in the outline and agree on which later section will be shortened.

When to refuse. Do not select vendors, queues, or shards before the workload and access paths exist. Avoid designing every optional feature or a multi-region disaster plan for a single-region MVP unless asked. A polished diagram is incomplete if no request was traced, no failure was considered, or no bottleneck was chosen for deeper analysis.
